title: “I feel like I am a warrior”: Sudanese women fight for peace on the front lines of war
text:
Three frontline responders tell UN Women what women and girls in Sudan need to heal themselves and their communities.

War was so far from Tahani Al-Numeiri’s reality that when she first heard explosions in her hometown Khartoum, she assumed they were celebrations from a wedding nearby. But as the gunfire and bombs drew closer, she soon realized her entire world was about to change.

Since then, when the war broke out in April 2023, more than one in four people in Sudan have been forced to flee their homes, surviving dangerous journeys in horrific conditions without access to food, water, health care, and protection.

For some, fleeing was not an option as they found themselves trapped in besieged areas unable to leave. Al-Numeiri and her family were among them.

“We thought the area where I was would never be taken over and that nothing bad would ever happen to us, so my family and I sat there hearing fighting, but it had not reached us yet. Maybe two months into the war, we found ourselves under siege; we could not get out”, remembers Al-Numeiri, a journalist and activist.

Until then, Al-Numeiri’s experience of war was limited to what she had seen on screen. “I never imagined my life would turn out just like in the movie,” she says.

Women and girls are surviving – and reemerging as frontline responders

Al-Numeiri described to UN Women staff in Sudan how communication networks collapsed, banking services became inaccessible, and essential supplies disappeared. She and her family were left with almost nothing to eat but boiled wheat, cooked on a fire. When they ran out of fuel, they burned their furniture to keep the fire going.

The conditions took a devastating toll on Al-Numeiri’s health. Malnutrition, contaminated water and the lack of medical care left her critically ill.

“My body was swollen, my skin was peeling, scabs were coming off. I had a severe fever, and there was blood in my eyes. I could not even see anyone next to me. My family had given up. They said I was going to die.”

But her sister kept encouraging her: “You are strong, girl.”

She would survive.

“Sunset came, then night, and I found myself still alive in my room”, says Al-Numeiri. Shortly after Khartoum was retaken, and as she recovered, she began putting her energy and strength into supporting others in her community – people who, just like her, had lived under siege.

It started in the communal kitchen where she was collecting food for her family – just two spoons of lentils. The woman running the kitchen learned Al-Numeiri was a journalist and encouraged her to post online about the conditions families were living in. “I stood with her, and the first video I filmed went viral – it showed that families in this area are hungry and thirsty.”

Al-Numeiri began to work as a volunteer in the kitchen while documenting the impact of the war on women and children in Sudan. She showed the world what was happening and helped mobilize support for those struggling to survive.

Al-Numeiri is one of the many women in Sudan who have emerged from this war as peacebuilders, mediators and frontline responders. They have supported their communities when the institutions around them have been destroyed. They have healed, led, rebuilt security, and stood for peace. Their experiences represent the toll of war on women and their communities – and the extraordinary resilience of women who refuse to surrender hope.

Women and girls continue to suffer – while funding for those that can help remains limited

Hundreds of kilometers from Khartoum lives Amna Mohamed** in the besieged city of El Fasher, which was taken over by the Rapid Support Forces in October 2025. Mohamed stayed in the city to continue serving her community.

Mohamed is the President of a women-led organization in North Darfur. Supported by UN Women, the organization – not named here, for people’s safety – offers meals through communal kitchens, organizes activities that promote peaceful coexistence and social cohesion, and gives financial support, including loans, to help women start up and sustain businesses.

Before the war, Mohamed was already working on peacebuilding and women’s empowerment. Then shelling and violence took over.

“Women were the first to suffer. They lost their husbands, children, and homes, and were left unprotected. At that point, the situation became catastrophic for women.” – Amna Mohamed**

“They may beat or rape you, and sometimes they loot your belongings. Sometimes they demand that you leave your home; they may kill your husband or brothers right before your eyes, or they may take your daughters right in front of you and lead them away to unknown locations. This is the situation we witnessed in El Fasher during the war.”

While many people fled El Fasher, those who were caring for elderly relatives, persons with disabilities or other dependents were unable to travel. Others simply didn’t have the money to hire a donkey or other transportation to leave, as they had exhausted their savings, trying to survive food shortages and soaring prices.

With nowhere to go, Mohamed described how they endured bombardments, dug trenches in their homes for protection and struggled to access food, water and healthcare.

“Despite everything, we held firm amid the gunfire, rockets, and artillery shelling all around us, but in the end, we had nothing left to eat or drink, and there were no basic services for the people.” – Amna Mohamed**

In a UN Women survey of 50 women’s organizations, one year after the takeover of El Fasher

Mohamed explains how some women have returned to El Fasher. “Some people have started to return, but doing so is risky due to the lack of security; there are no security guarantees, and women who have returned have been raped.”

The conditions in El Fasher remain horrific.

“Hospitals are being rehabilitated, but many remain out of service. Some doctors and medications have arrived, but they are insufficient and limited. Most of them are emergency medications”, explains Mohamed.

It’s not just healthcare that is limited. The needs remain colossal.

“Women need ways to earn a living to buy food, drink, and other necessities, as well as clothing and household items. They also need containers to carry water because accessing drinking water is challenging; water sources are sometimes far away, making fetching water time-consuming. The girls also need sanitary pads, which help them maintain their dignity.”

“Our relationship with women is direct and close, and as women-led organizations, we are best positioned to serve them; we understand their needs. However, when it comes to funding, projects sometimes go to organizations led by men.” – Amna Mohamed**

There is no recovery without psychological healing

Back in Khartoum, thousands of women are also returning after years of displacement across Sudan and in neighbouring countries. At the UN Women-supported East Nile Women’s Empowerment Centre in Khartoum, women are beginning the long and complicated road to recovery as they start to rebuild their homes and communities.

Psychosocial support officer Israa Hamid Khalil is helping them. Alongside counselling and psychosocial care, women are offered training and livelihood support to earn an income and support their families.

“After they returned home, women came back with nothing at their hands, they lost everything”, explains Khalil. “Right now, our focus is on [them]. We are trying to alleviate the suffering that they have endured during the war and during their displacement from the Khartoum area and other regions to find safety and peace.”

Khalil told UN Women that women were dealing with trauma from the early stages of the war, and what happened during their displacement. Now home, they have found their houses looted, stripped of everything they owned, even the doors and windows.

title: Sudan: Nine in 10 organizations say trauma persists among women and girls displaced from El Fasher a year after its fall
text:
Remarks by Anna Mutavati, UN Women Regional Director for East and Southern Africa, to whom quoted text may be attributed, at press briefing at the Palais des Nations in Geneva

Khartoum/Geneva/Nairobi – “A year ago, the world watched as atrocities in El Fasher, North Darfur, were livestreamed to our phones.

A year later, the impact of violence, and the risk of renewed violence remains.

And across Sudan, drone attacks are increasing across Blue Nile State, Khartoum, West Kordofan, Gedaref State, and the Khashm al-Girba area in Kassala State. Most of those killed or injured are women and children. Many had already fled violence, including sexual violence, seeking safety or attempting to return home.

The images that emerged from El Fasher a year ago offered a window into the extent to which violence in Sudan is inflicted on women and girls – gang raped, beaten, humiliated and robbed of their belongings. Some were taken and have not been seen since.

UN Women conducted a survey of 50 women’s organizations supporting people displaced from El Fasher. I am sharing the results with you today.

One year on, the scars of the violence in El Fasher have not faded. Women and girls continue to live with the trauma of sexual violence, the disappearance of their daughters, sisters, mothers, husbands and sons, the killing of family members, and the loss of their homes and livelihoods.

Psychological distress, sleepless nights and unsafe living conditions are part of daily life, and so is the struggle to find food, water, and healthcare.

Safety is mostly out of reach.

Nine in ten organizations we surveyed described displaced women and girls living in unsafe living conditions. Forty-nine of 50 organizations observed signs of psychological distress among women and girls displaced from El Fasher, and 45 of them – 90 per cent – reported that this distress persists today. Forty-eight of 50 organizations report women being unable to sleep because of the trauma they have experienced.

Around two-thirds of organizations we spoke to were aware of women or girls who disappeared during or after the fall of El Fasher.

The needs of women and girls are immense but access to support is severely limited.

Forty-three of the 50 organizations had encountered women or girls in distress who had received no mental health, psychosocial or legal support since fleeing, and nearly half said few or none of the women they work with could access such support.

Critical service providers, including those providing mental health and health care are facing threats of arrest and harassment while delivering services – all in the absence of protection.

Some people have started to return to El Fasher, but the fear of violence is constant.

According to the 2026 Sudan Multi-Sectoral Needs Assessment by IOM[1], 84 per cent of 117 households surveyed in Al Fasher said women avoid marketplaces, two thirds avoid collecting firewood, while half avoid social, community or religious spaces.

We are hearing reports of hospitals lacking doctors and medicines needed to function beyond emergency cases. Food and access to other basic goods are also scarce.

Across Sudan, we are seeing an increase in drone attacks on displacement camps, markets and other civilian infrastructure, leaving those fleeing with no safe space to turn and with total disregard for international humanitarian law.

Attacks on civilian infrastructure kill and injure civilians and add to the difficulties they face in accessing essential services and livelihoods, and force more people to flee. The UN Fact-Finding Mission found that 80 per cent of hospitals in conflict-affected areas are not functioning, causing a spike in maternal deaths and reducing women’s access to sexual and reproductive health care.

But there is another side to this war that is rarely told. The emergence of women across Sudan as front-line responders, caregivers, mediators, and peacebuilders. They are doing so as the institutions around them have collapsed, and as persistent underfunding and insecurity threaten their work. Supported by UN Women, these women-led organizations reach communities others cannot, and are a lifeline to women and girls, their families and communities.

Across Sudan, UN Women provides lifesaving support to women and girls and invests in women’s leadership – which is critical for peace, security, and recovery. We work with grassroots women’s networks to strengthen their capacity for dialogue, negotiation, conflict analysis, mediation and advocacy, enabling women to resolve disputes, reduce tensions and influence the decisions shaping their communities.

As we mark 26 years since the adoption of Security Council resolution 1325, which laid the foundation for the Women, Peace and Security agenda, the experiences of women in Sudan, and their role in the country’s peace and security are central to this commitment.

UN Women calls for the protection of civilians, accountability for perpetrators of violence, and compliance with international humanitarian and human rights law. Women and girls must have access to essential services and resources and participate meaningfully in decisions about peace and their country’s future, with sustained support for the women leaders and organizations working on the front lines.”

[1] IOM Multi-Sectoral Needs Assessment 2026

title: Sudan: El Fasher civilians suffer unlawful killings, detention and torture one year after city’s capture by the RSF – new testimony
text:
Surveillance and detentions rife in city

With limited humanitarian aid, risks of child malnutrition remain high

“A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today” – Agnès Callamard

Civilians in El Fasher in North Darfur, Sudan, are still suffering detention, torture and limited access to humanitarian aid one year after the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) captured the city and committed brutalities against civilians, Amnesty International said today.

In new testimony, residents who recently escaped the city told Amnesty International how schools had been turned into detention centres, how their movement was strictly controlled, and that unlawful killings were rife.

According to figures gathered by humanitarian organizations working in the city, fewer than 70,000 people are present in El Fasher, compared to its pre-war population of more than one million. Humanitarian access remains limited, and humanitarian workers and other civilians in the city are constantly surveilled or monitored. Arbitrary detention risks, for both civilians and humanitarian workers, remain extremely high.

A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today

Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General

“The RSF’s claims that El Fasher is safe for civilians to return to after the horrific massacres that took place one year ago could not be further from the truth,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.

“A pervasive pall of fear hangs over El Fasher today. Men and women live under constant RSF surveillance, and with the ongoing threat of detention, torture and killing.

“One year since El Fasher fell to the RSF, the international community has failed to take the necessary actions to address the desperate plight civilians face as the conflict rages. There has been little accountability for abuses in North Darfur. The moves towards a ceasefire have been half-hearted, and Amnesty International is not aware of any diplomatic attempts to establish an international force that would meaningfully protect civilians.

“Crucially, the United Arab Emirates has continued to support the RSF, while governments with the required influence have largely failed to name and denounce their role or hold them to account.

“Without a ceasefire, accountability, and a protection force, civilians will continue to suffer in El Fasher and across Sudan. The Sudanese Armed Forces have consistently opposed the extension of an arms embargo and a ceasefire, continuing to believe that a military ‘solution’ to the conflict remains possible, thereby also setting aside the suffering of the Sudanese people.”

In August and September 2026, Amnesty International interviewed 25 civilians, including 19 residents and six humanitarian workers, regarding the situation in El Fasher. Of the residents, 15 left El Fasher between July and August 2026 and one was still in the city; the other three had fled earlier.

On 9 October, Amnesty International wrote to the RSF regarding the findings. At the time of publication, no response had been received.

In July 2026, Amnesty International released a major report that documented how the RSF committed crimes against humanity and ethnic cleansing during its campaign to seize El Fasher, with certain ethnic groups, including the Zaghawa, singled out for abuse. Amnesty International continues to document flagrant abuses committed by both parties to the conflict in Sudan, including in El Obeid, North Kordofan, as well as in South Kordofan and Blue Nile States.

Detention, torture, and unlawful killings in prisons

Of the 19 residents interviewed, 17 were detained by the RSF. Most were arbitrarily detained during the RSF capture of the city, while several were detained when they returned to retrieve belongings from their homes or to search for missing family members. They were all held in captivity for months. Several noted that people of particular ethnic groups, notably Zaghawa and Masalit people, were more likely to be detained and abused.

Most men were held in detention centres or prisons, where they witnessed unlawful killings, suffered torture and other ill-treatment, and were given minimal food or water. All were released only after family members paid ransom, or by escaping.

If you sleep a lot, they don’t like that, they will execute you

Modathir*, a 29-year-old Zaghawa man, who was detained in Shala prison

Modathir*, a 29-year-old Zaghawa man, was detained in Shala prison. He was regularly beaten and witnessed unlawful killings. He told Amnesty International: “Torture is something which is permanent in any [RSF] detention. They executed people who tried to look at them… If you sleep a lot, they don’t like that, they will execute you. They ask, ‘You want to take a rest? We will give you permanent rest’.” In July 2026, Modathir escaped, fleeing from house to house in order to reach safety.

Mamoun*, a 33-year-old Zaghawa man, was also held in Shala prison until July 2026. He said he witnessed the RSF shooting prisoners, and the death of a man with untreated diabetes who the RSF refused to help. Mamoun was regularly beaten, and said: “They take people out [of the cell] randomly, they accuse you of being with the Joint Forces or the military… And they beat you until you faint… Sometimes I was beaten four times a day… It just depends on their mood.” Mamoun was eventually released after his family paid a ransom.

Paying ransom was not always a guarantee of freedom. Musa*, a 23-year-old Zaghawa man, said that he and his father were detained at El Fasher Children’s Hospital in October 2025. They were released more than a month later after they paid a ransom. However, instead of being allowed to leave the city, Musa said the RSF took them to an RSF-guarded house and held there until around May 2026 when they were able to escape.

Musa and his father were forced to work for the RSF including collecting corpses, and were sometimes forced to speak on camera to say that the city was inhabitable, encouraging people to return. He said: “They paraded us inside the city and told us to talk [about how] El Fasher is good and safe.”

Detention in schools

Women, children, and some older or injured men were held in schools that were de facto detention centres. They described high rates of malnutrition, including among their own children.

Amnesty International interviewed nine people who were detained by the RSF in schools. They had extremely limited access to food and medical treatment; some women said that their children became malnourished during their detention there. All of these individuals were released or managed to escape by July or August 2026.

Haram*, a 45-year-old Zaghawa woman, and her young children were detained at a school in the Daraja Oula neighbourhood. She told Amnesty International: “[The RSF] were verbally abusing people… Zaghawa people were beaten, [the RSF] would just select and randomly beat [people]. They called us falangayaat women [a slur that indicates slavery or servitude].”

Hadia*, a 30-year-old Gimir woman whose husband was shot by the RSF during their capture of El Fasher, was detained in a school with her children, along with hundreds of other women and children. The RSF provided them very limited food and water.

Hadia was too malnourished to provide her youngest child, aged 18 months, with sufficient breast milk. When she finally escaped and reached Tawila in August 2026, all three of her children were diagnosed with malnutrition; one was hospitalized. Hadia told Amnesty International: “My children were very skinny and weak.”

Aloya*, a 54-year-old Zaghawa woman, spent several months detained in a school. She was afraid that her Zaghawa identity would be discovered and so never spoke the language while there. She said: “Daily there were four to five people dying… mostly from lack of food.”

title: Sudan: Aerial attacks on populated areas are endangering civilian lives [EN/AR]
source: International Committee of the Red Cross
text:
Port Sudan (ICRC) - In recent weeks, aerial attacks across Sudan have caused a worrying increase in civilian harm. Most of the attacks were likely carried out by armed drones.

Residential areas, markets and areas sheltering displaced populations have been particularly affected, with hundreds of people reportedly killed. This raises grave concerns about the protection of civilians and risks aggravating the world’s largest humanitarian crisis.

“The use of drones does not change the rules of war. Technology does not absolve those who use it of their obligations under international humanitarian law,” said Lorenzo Caraffi, the International Committee of the Red Cross’s (ICRC) Head of Delegation in Sudan.

Under international humanitarian law, those who plan, authorize or carry out attacks must always distinguish between civilians and military targets. Indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks are prohibited. All feasible precautions to avoid or minimize civilian harm must be taken.

The ICRC is supporting hospitals across Sudan with essential medical supplies, specialist surgical teams and other assistance to help absorb the influx of war-wounded. In the first half of 2026, ICRC-supported hospitals recorded over 2,700 weapon wounded patients.

The ICRC urges all sides to take into account the foreseeable humanitarian consequences of using armed drones, particularly in populated areas.

title: From Safety Risks to Action - GBV Safety Audit Report - Tawila Locality, North Darfur State, Sudan (September 2026)
source: Gender Based Violence Area of Responsibility, Protection Cluster, United Nations Population Fund
text:
The Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Safety Audit for Tawila locality, North Darfur, was conducted in September 2026 under the technical guidance of UNFPA, in collaboration with GBV and protection partners. As a follow-up to the June 2026 audit, it covered a larger number of IDP camps, gathering sites and host-community locations. It aimed to identify GBV and protection risks affecting women, adolescent girls, children, persons with disabilities and newly displaced populations, and to inform safer humanitarian programming.

The audit identified serious and interconnected protection concerns. These include:

widespread lack of night lighting

shelters without locks or privacy, including shared living arrangements for unaccompanied children

unsafe and non-private latrines and showers

risks linked to firewood collection and income-generating activities outside the camps

safety and fairness concerns at distributions

gaps in 24/7 health care, clinical management of rape and confidential referral

Girls were reported to face greater barriers than women across all services assessed.

The report calls for coordinated, multi-sectoral action across GBV, Protection, Child Protection, WASH, Health, Shelter/NFI, CCCM, Food Security and other relevant sectors. Key recommendations include:

improving lighting, WASH safety and shelter privacy

strengthening health facility readiness and emergency referral

making distributions safer, with stronger PSEA and accountability measures

expanding safe spaces and confidential reporting

prioritizing adolescent girls, women with disabilities, female-headed households and newly displaced people

The Safety Audit provides a shared evidence base for funded, site-specific action plans and for tracking progress on GBV risk mitigation across the humanitarian response in Tawila.

title: From Safety Risks to Action - GBV Safety Audit Report - El Obeid, North Kordofan State, Sudan (September 2026)
source: Gender Based Violence Area of Responsibility, Protection Cluster, United Nations Population Fund
text:
The Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Safety Audit for El Obeid, Sheikan Locality, North Kordofan, was conducted in September 2026 by UNFPA in collaboration with Plan International and JASMAR Human Security Organization. It covered eight IDP gathering points. The assessment examined how living conditions, site layout, access routes and the availability of services affect the safety of displaced women and girls, with the aim of informing practical risk-mitigation measures.

The audit identified a range of protection concerns. These include:

poor lighting and unsafe movement after dark

inadequate or distant latrines and bathing facilities, and water shortages

overcrowded and damaged shelters with limited privacy

gaps in health, maternal health and MHPSS services, and weak referral pathways

a lack of dedicated safe spaces for women and girls

congestion and unclear beneficiary lists at distribution points

Taqat, the Unified Camp and Police Camp were identified as requiring particular attention.

The report calls for coordinated action across site management, WASH, Health, Shelter, Protection/GBV and Education. Key recommendations include:

installing lighting along key routes

expanding safe, accessible and sex-segregated sanitation facilities

establishing Women and Girls Safe Spaces and confidential referral pathways

improving access to health and MHPSS services

applying protection-sensitive procedures to distributions and shelter planning

The Safety Audit provides an evidence base for prioritizing site-level improvements and tracking follow-up actions to make daily life safer for displaced women and girls in El Obeid.

title: Sudan Operation - Coordination Meeting Minutes - Port Sudan and Khartoum, 20 October 2026
text:
OCHA Access Update

The OCHA Access Unit provided an update on humanitarian access conditions across Sudan.

Conditions continue to evolve in Darfur, Kordofan, and Blue Nile, with implications for humanitarian operations and access. Physical access in parts of Darfur has improved over the past year, with many areas now more accessible than at the same time last year, allowing humanitarian organizations to reach locations that were previously difficult to access or entirely inaccessible. Furthermore, the rainy season has not resulted in significant disruptions to movement, as below-average rainfall this year has had a limited impact on road conditions.

Partners raised concerns related to approvals, registrations, and other administrative impediments affecting humanitarian operations and requiring follow-up.

Partners were encouraged to report access constraints through the Access Reporting Tool (ART).

Operational Updates | Logistics

The LTC thanked partners for their participation in the Cluster Coordination Performance Monitoring (CCPM) survey. Analysis is underway and results will be shared in the next coordination meeting.

Common Services

The LTC reminded partners that transport support is available as a last resort on a case-by-case basis, based on prioritized localities.

The LTC reminded partners of the following ongoing expansion of common storage services:

Port Sudan: An additional 250 m2 of temperature-controlled storage is being added, bringing the total capacity to 604 m2.

El Obeid: An additional 1,110 m2 of storage capacity is being added through the WFP cooperating partner, bringing the total capacity to 1,600 m2. Kosti continues to be recommended for longer-term cargo prepositioning.

Central Darfur: The LTC is progressing the expansion to three additional storage locations (Nertiti, Golo, and Rokero). Partners will be informed as soon as the facilities are operational.

For any questions related to common services, or support with Service Request Forms (SRFs), partners are encouraged to contact sudan.clustercargo@wfp.org.

Convoys

The LTC continues to support the coordination of convoy movements, with WFP-led convoys organized from Kosti, Ad Dabbah and Farchana to priority locations in the Kordofan and Darfur regions. Partners are reminded to express their interest in joining convoys as early as possible. Transit times vary based on destination, access and security conditions, route accessibility, and administrative requirements.

Partners were encouraged to submit expressions of interest in advance and preposition cargo in Kosti and/or Ad Dabbah to facilitate timely participation.

Upcoming convoy opportunities will continue to be communicated through the mailing list and WhatsApp group. For any questions related to convoy coordination, contact sudan.clustercargo@wfp.org.

Information Management

Partners were reminded that information products containing key operational information are regularly published on the Logistics Cluster website and mobile application. Recent publications include:

Situation Update: Adre Border Crossing Extended Until 31 December 2026

WFP Market Monitor: October 2026

UNHAS Sudan Weekly Flight Schedule Effective 1-30 November 2026

Logistics Cluster Brochure (English & Arabic)

Infographic – January to July 2026

To receive real-time alerts when new products and coordination meeting invites are published, partners were encouraged to download the Logistics Cluster mobile application and follow the Sudan operation.

Other support available

Partners were informed about a potential maritime transport opportunity from France to Port Sudan coordinated through Hulo. Hulo confirmed that the initiative remains under consultation, and that operational details, routing, container configuration, and schedules have not yet been confirmed.

The deadline for submissions via the Transport by hulo platform is COB Thursday, 22 October 2026.

The Hulo communication was circulated through the mailing list. For any questions, partners were encouraged to contact Hulo directly at euhab@hulo.coop.

Operational Updates | Telecommunications

LTC encouraged partners to complete the Telecoms Area User Satisfaction Survey. Feedback will support future service planning and prioritization. The deadline is 28 October 2026. If facing any issues accessing the survey, try using a VPN.

Partners were reminded to ensure that Starlink equipment is properly registered and that appropriate enterprise subscription arrangements are in place, as the current grace period is expected to end in November 2026. Organizations using residential subscriptions were advised to migrate to appropriate enterprise subscriptions. For further guidance, including available local connectivity options, contact sudan.etc@wfp.org.

In Geneina, internet connectivity services are available at the IMC compound and will be extended to NRC facilities. Additional assessments are underway in Nertiti and Tawila. In Khartoum, internet connectivity services are available at the IOM and WFP offices.

Organizations seeking backup connectivity solutions were encouraged to submit requests to sudan.etc@wfp.org.

In eastern Sudan, telecommunications services remain operational in Port Sudan, Kassala, Gedaref, Damazine, and Kosti.

Efforts are ongoing to reactivate the security telecommunications network in Khartoum, pending the necessary approvals.

An LTC Telecoms mission is planned to El Obeid, North Kordofan. Partners wishing to meet with the team or discuss connectivity requirements are encouraged to contact sudan.etc@wfp.org, copying karen.barsamian@wfp.org.

During LTC Telecoms Coordinator Yousif Mirza’s break-in-service, Karen Barsamian, WFP Head of TEC, will serve as the primary focal point for LTC Telecoms.

Services for Communities (S4C)

The Community Service Centre in Khartoum remains operational, providing affected communities with access to power and internet connectivity. More than 2,300 beneficiaries accessed the service during the previous month.

Discussions are ongoing with the Ministry of Education and the Education Cluster to explore a potential initiative to rehabilitate computer laboratories at the University of Khartoum.

The Ministry of Health (MoH) and Health Cluster are exploring a connectivity support initiative aimed at strengthening communications infrastructure in government health facilities.

WFP On-Demand Services (ODS)

WFP reminded partners that On-Demand Services (ODS) are available to the humanitarian community on a full cost-recovery basis.

Organizations wishing to access ODS support are required to sign a Service Level Agreement (SLA) with WFP prior to service delivery.

Fuel requests are managed through the Service Marketplace (SMP), while transportation requests are processed through the UN Booking Hub.

Partners requiring support with the platform or service requests were encouraged to contact the ODS team directly.

title: Sudan: UNISFA statement on drone strikes at Amiet Market in Abyei (Updated - 22 October 2026)
source: UN Interim Security Force for Abyei
text:
Abyei, 21 October 2026 – **Abyei

Update on the situation in Abyei: Following the Secretary-General's condemnation of the drone attacks in Abyei on 19 October, the UN Interim Force there, our peacekeeping force, UNISFA, tells us that at least 80 people were killed, with 27 injured treated by UN personnel. The Mission continues to verify casualties, and other people are still missing.

UNISFA has extinguished the major fires caused by the attacks on Amiet Market and Todach, with our peacekeepers continue to evacuate casualties and provide medical assistance. UN Mine Action personnel are also assessing the affected areas for any unexploded ordnance.

The Mission has also doubled its patrols in the affected areas to help deter further violence and is engaging with community leaders to encourage restraint and prevent retaliation.

UNISFA continues to engage with the Governments of Sudan, South Sudan and other relevant stakeholders in an effort to support the de-escalation. We reiterate the Secretary-General's call on both Governments to take all possible steps to prevent further attacks and uphold Abyei's demilitarized status, while maintaining dialogue through existing mechanisms, including at the upcoming Joint Political and Security Mechanism meeting that is scheduled in Khartoum.

**Sudan Consultations

On Sudan, but turning to Geneva, as we’ve told you, we are co-hosting along with the Government of Switzerland the sixth round of the consultations on Sudan among international and regional actors trying to work together to end this devastating war.

At the “Sixth Consultative Meeting on Enhancing Coordination of Peace Initiatives and Efforts for Sudan,” Mr. Pekka Haavisto, the Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy, said that the meeting offers an opportunity to take stock of our collective efforts and consider how to strengthen coordination among the respective initiatives.

The sessions aim to explore practical ways forward, including a path towards a transitional political phase that reflects the aspirations of the Sudanese people. A key focus will be laying the foundations for an inclusive and credible dialogue that can advantage a Sudanese-led political process.

Mr. Haavisto added that it is also essential to listen to the perspectives of countries in the region and consider how to prevent further deterioration and spillovers.

Mr. Haavisto affirmed his commitment to convening these meetings every three months to maintain momentum and help develop pragmatic responses to an evolving situation.

Q&A

Question: Thank you, Steph. One follow-up on Abyei and then a question. On Abyei, has there been any determination of who was responsible for this deadly attack?

Spokesperson: We are not at this point able to make a formal determination.

[…]

Question: Thank you, Stéphane. A follow-up on the meeting in Geneva. So after this meeting and after, as you said, the parties taking part in this meeting would have unified a vision or a plan, does the UN intend to present this plan to the warring parties to talk about, or does it plan to start a negotiation process?

Spokesperson: I don't think I said that the outcome of the meeting would be a unified plan. That is the effort to keep going. I'm not -- let's wait for the meeting to conclude. But from what I understand, with my limited understanding of things, I'm not expecting a full announcement, in the sense that you said. The aim of the meeting, as Mr. Haavisto said, is to explore practical ways forward in how we can advance towards a transitional political phase that takes very much into account, puts at the centre the aspirations of the Sudanese people. I would also encourage you to watch the press conference, which I think may either still be going on or just concluded a little while ago by Mr. Haavisto in Geneva.

title: Sudan: Drone strikes killed at least 306 people in three weeks
text:
UN human rights chief Volker Türk on Friday strongly condemned an escalation in drone strikes across Sudan this month, which killed at least 306 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October alone.

The strikes, attributed to both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), hit homes, markets, hospitals, displacement sites, power stations and water sources in Kordofan, Darfur, Blue Nile, Khartoum and other states, according to the UN human rights office (OHCHR).

“The increasing use of drones, already accounting for the majority of conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan this year, is deeply disturbing and is exacting a horrifying toll,” Mr. Türk said.

In a particularly disturbing trend, the office documented numerous strikes on displacement sites, where people who had already fled the fighting had sought shelter.

Between 6 and 10 October, alleged drone strikes attributed to military government forces on shelters for displaced people in Ghubeish and El Nuhud in West Kordofan killed at least 25 civilians, including women and children.

On 9 October, an alleged RSF drone struck a crowd of displaced people engaged in artisanal gold mining near a displacement site in Abu Shendi, Blue Nile, killing at least 31 people, most of them women and children.

On 18 October, at least 139 people were killed when a transportation truck was hit in a “double tap” repeat strike in Dibab, West Kordofan, an area controlled by the RSF militia.

Markets and hospitals have also been hit, including an RSF-attributed strike on Um Darfa hospital in Blue Nile on 11 October that seriously injured two health workers and left the facility non-operational.

“Scores of civilians have been killed, including internally displaced persons, and vital infrastructure and services have been eviscerated, driving further displacement and deepening the already severe humanitarian crisis,” said OHCHR Spokesperson Seif Magango.

Peacekeepers with the UN Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) this week visited communities affected by a drone attack on 19 October on Amiet Market and the Todach area in Abyei, the disputed oil-rich region between Sudan and South Sudan. The attack killed more than 80 people.

UNISFA troops were the first to reach the scene, where “every shop was burning”, said Lieutenant Colonel Muhammad Farooq, commander of the Mission’s Pakistani battalion.

The Mission deployed quick reaction and firefighting teams to stop the fire spreading and took more than 27 injured people to its hospital in Todach, according to Acting Force Commander Brigadier General Adebowale Ajabge.

Angelina Musa Diaw, a trader and mother of three, said she had lost everything. “No work, everything is gone,” she said. “I am here with my children. But I need help.”

In a statement released Friday, the Security Council condemned the Abyei attack “in the strongest terms”, warning that the death toll is expected to rise as UNISFA continues to verify casualties. They stressed that attacks on civilians could amount to war crimes and called for a full, transparent and prompt investigation, with those responsible held to account.

The council reaffirmed that Abyei must remain demilitarized and free of all forces except UNISFA, and called on all actors to end military operations and occupation in the area. Members urged all parties to work with the Mission to protect civilians, aid workers and peacekeepers.

Mr. Türk called on the parties to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law (IHL), including by not directing attacks against civilians and civilian objects.

“Broader peace efforts must squarely address the continued influx of arms that is fuelling the conflict and press for an end to the transfer of arms that are used in manifest disregard of the IHL obligations protecting civilians,” he said.

“I urge both parties to the conflict, and their affiliates, to commit to a ceasefire,” the High Commissioner added, stressing that a negotiated settlement with human rights at its core, underpinned by accountability, is the only feasible pathway to sustainable peace in Sudan.

title: In-Depth Gender-Sensitive Joint Labour Market Assessment (LMA), Sudan | EMPOWER Programme
source: Danish Refugee Council, IMPACT Initiatives, Mercy Corps
text:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Sudan is experiencing one of the most severe humanitarian crises in the world, driven by the armed conflict that erupted in April 2023. The conflict has triggered one of the largest displacement crises globally, with over 15 million people displaced as of April 2026. Widespread destruction of economic infrastructure and key productive sectors has dramatically reduced livelihood opportunities and shrunk labour demand across the country. Conflict dynamics, population movement, inflation, supply chain disruptions and fragmented governance have further constrained the labour market, with per capita income having fallen from USD 3,400 in 2022 to USD 2,000 in 2024, a level not seen since 1992. Youth aged 15 to 35 primarily bear a disproportionate share of these pressures; they already faced structural barriers to employment before the conflict, including weak private sector development, limited job creation, and a persistent mismatch between education systems and labour market needs.

Despite the scale of these challenges, the evidence base on youth labour markets in Sudan remains fragmented. With almost 20 livelihood zones and significant regional divergence across states, existing data is insufficient to inform targeted, context-specific programming. In particular, there is a critical gap in up-todate, localised evidence on viable livelihood opportunities, sector-specific labour demand, and the constraints facing Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in sustaining or expanding employment. Against this backdrop, the Enabling Market Pathways and Opportunities for Work, Economic Recovery and Resilience (EMPOWER) programme, led by the Danish Refugee Council (DRC) and Mercy Corps in partnership with Sudanese NGOs and funded by the European Union (EU), commissioned an In-Depth Gender-Sensitive Joint Labour Market Assessment (LMA), in collaboration with IMPACT Initiatives. The assessment examined labour supply and demand, skills gaps, workforce capacity and broader market systems across nine target states to inform livelihood-pathway prioritisation. Using a mixed-methods, Market Systems Development (MSD) approach, the assessment combined secondary data with 2,814 youth and 936 employer/MSME surveys, 66 key informant interviews and 54 focus group discussions. Data were collected across 18 localities in nine states between July and August 2026.

The findings highlight that a majority of youth in the study areas were not engaged in employment or income-generating activities. Over half of respondents (59%) were not working, and 58% of these had never worked, a share far higher among young women (70%) than young men (33%). Employment is predominantly informal and self-arranged, led by self-employment (47%) and casual daily labour (26%). Trade accounted for the largest reported share of youth employment (35%), with petty trade the most commonly reported economic activity. Petty trade was also the activity most frequently identified by both female (64%) and male (65%) youth as a suitable business or employment option, indicating strong interest in accessible forms of self-employment and income generation. Among working youth, 47% of those in services and 45% of crop farmers said their skills fully match their work, against 37% of petty traders. Nepotism and favouritism were the most frequently reported institutional or systemic barriers to employment (41%).

Employer survey data covers four broad sectors: services (35%), trade (30%), manufacturing (15%) and agriculture (13%), and points to considerable variation in hiring potential and job quality. Services show the strongest overall employment potential, combining an established business base (43% operating for more than six years), comparatively high recruitment (46% hiring in the past 12 months) and a higher concentration of young workers, though access remains heavily skewed towards young men. Trade was the sector with the most readily available entry point into the labour market and is reported by youth to be the most accessible sector, but low hiring and a limited share of larger employers indicate a limited potential for expanding wage employment. The manufacturing sector has the largest share of MSMEs and the highest demand for technical and skilled workers, but youth and women’s representation in the workforce remains low. Agriculture remains an established and relatively stable sector, aligned with the agropastoral landscape of Sudan, with a high demand for casual labour; active youth participation is comparatively limited, linked to displacement and access constraints.

Across all sectors, employers report substantial difficulty in recruiting suitably skilled workers (44% overall), and youth confirm the gap: only a third (32%) say their skills fully match available opportunities. These differences point to the importance of tailoring skills development and employment interventions to sector-specific labour demand rather than relying on a single skills or training model across locations. Employers’ capacity to create new vacancies is constrained, most often by limited access to finance (61%), followed by weak business growth (43%) and high labour costs (33%). These findings suggest that addressing youth employment constraints will require not only investments in young people’s skills and employability but also measures that address the financial and operational constraints limiting employers’ capacity to recruit and train youth.

Market and institutional constraints further affect the ability of businesses to create and sustain employment. Financial services (37%) and market information (36%) were the most commonly reported support services accessed by employers, while the support employers say would most help them hire or train youth is wage subsidies (62%), access to finance for the business (53%) and equipment and tools (44%), while taxation and fees were the most frequently reported policy and regulatory barrier (52%). At the broader market level, the conflict has increased transaction costs by an estimated 30–40% and contributed to a reported 45% decline in formal cross-border trade, further limiting market access and increasing the costs and risks of business operations. Despite these constraints, 58% of employers expressed willingness to participate in employment-creation interventions, indicating potential scope for employer engagement in initiatives that address both workforce and business constraints.

Findings on viable pathways to employment indicate two limiting factors that are reported across the assessed states and sectors: access to finance and the availability of workers with the specific skills employers need. Agriculture shows convergence across the three states where it is a priority or promising pathway, with casual labour demand and finance identified as key barriers in all of them. In services, finance and weak business growth are the leading employer constraints in Gedaref and North Kordofan, and weak business growth in Kassala; in all three, employers report relatively little difficulty finding candidates, which points to a constraint on employers’ capacity to offer secure, well-paid roles rather than a skills gap; in River Nile and South Darfur, by contrast, hiring difficulty is high (62% and 51%), making services there a skillsmatching case. The trade sector (promising in two states) combines strong income adequacy with hiring difficulty, indicating an accessible but largely informal pathway.
