title: The Sudan Humanitarian Fund: A Pooled Fund in Transition
text:
By Nicholas Noe , Hala Eltom , Yousra Semmache | October 22, 2026

Sudan is the largest humanitarian crisis in the world, and the Sudan Humanitarian Fund (SHF) is now operating at an unprecedented scale for a UN Regional or Country-Based Pooled Fund (R/CBPF). How the SHF spends its money will help decide whether localization of the relief effort in Sudan – shifting power and resources to local and national responders – becomes a reality. The Fund’s direction will also shape how well the next phase of the response copes with deeply troubling humanitarian trends.

The Fund’s growth is all the more striking because the wider response is shrinking, even as needs reach record levels. In 2026, an estimated 33.7 million people, nearly two-thirds of Sudan’s population, will need assistance. Yet the humanitarian response plan has been cut to a “basic survival package.” By September 2026, the plan was only 41 percent funded. Of the roughly $1.12 billion received, $457 million, more than two-fifths, flowed through the SHF.

The SHF has real achievements when it comes to localization. Its Emergency Response Room/Mutual Aid Group (ERR/MAG) program grew from $15 million in 2024 to $25 million in 2025–2026, sending small, flexible grants to frontline responders. The Fund has also handed two of the program’s six intermediary roles to national NGOs. And it now requires lead partners to pass the full 7 percent overhead on to every sub-grantee, a reform that has not yet spread across the global pooled-fund system.

Yet on direct funding, the SHF has lagged behind its peers. According to OCHA’s CBPF Data Hub, only about 6 percent of SHF funding went directly to Sudanese actors in 2025, rising to about 27 percent when subgrants (indirect funding) are counted.1 Both figures were the lowest among the roughly two dozen pooled funds we compared. Across OCHA pooled funds, around 55 percent reach local and national actors when subgrants are included.

A key reason was the narrow pipeline of eligible local partners. In 2024, the Fund invited 62 national NGOs into its onboarding process. By year’s end, just two had been accepted. By the end of 2025, the Fund had only 25 Sudanese partners, and only six received direct grants. This small partner pool concentrated influence among a few Sudanese organizations. The same three national representatives sat on the Fund’s Advisory Board for years without rotation. Women-led organizations have fared poorly. None of the 13 prioritized in 2024 completed onboarding that year.

In interviews, stakeholders repeatedly named four main barriers to entry:

registration with the federal Humanitarian Aid Commission (HAC).

The first three are technical and can be solved by drawing on the experience of other pooled funds. HAC registration is more challenging. It must be renewed every year and is not realistically obtainable for many groups in a country de facto split between the control of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Many groups working outside areas controlled by SAF, or fearing harassment, cannot safely register at all.

Behind these numbers lay a deeper problem. For years, the prevailing view at the SHF was that investing in the institutional capacity of local partners was not the Fund’s job. Yet pooled funds routinely pay for the far more expensive institutional structures of UN agencies and international NGOs. Refusing to invest in local actors does not save money. Rather, it can lock in costlier delivery models that leave less for affected communities. In Ukraine, by contrast, early investment in national NGOs – few of which had any experience in humanitarian operations before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 – built a broad pool of local partners and freed up tens of millions of dollars for lifesaving aid.

The good news is that new UN leadership in Sudan has made localization a top priority over the last year. This came despite a setback. When a major U.S. contribution arrived in early 2026, none of the first $195 million in allocations went directly to Sudanese actors, partly because of OCHA’s tight six-month spending deadline. The SHF responded with a $40 million allocation in June 2026 that gave national NGOs priority for direct funding. It also introduced dedicated “Localization Costs” in project budgets. As of September 2026, the partner pool of Sudanese NGOs has grown from 25 to 33, including several that had failed onboarding for years despite managing tens of millions of dollars in aid. Six new Sudanese NGOs have taken up seats on the Advisory Board.

OCHA headquarters also recognizes the need for a course correction. Its guidance for the second U.S. tranche of $175 million calls for doubling national NGO seats on Advisory Boards from three to six. It also supports “passporting” capacity assessments, tiered eligibility, and microgrants of up to $10,000. UN agencies and INGOs can no longer charge senior management and headquarters staff costs, while local and national actors can. Separately, the SHF has offered up to $1 million for a Sudanese-led localization process. This could reshape the response, but only if the Fund’s role as funder stays clearly separate from Sudanese ownership of the process.

None of this will be easy. Fund managers face intense pressure from UN agencies and INGOs whose core budgets have been cut. International actors also bring real advantages. But OCHA’s guidance reinforces steps the SHF has already taken and should make it easier to go further. To this end, the SHF should open more routes to direct funding for local groups. It should offer longer-term funding and help organizations that fail assessments improve rather than shutting them out. Local actors should have more say in SHF allocations.

Finally, the SHF should engage a new, potentially more transformational channel for local funding. Over the last few years, nearly 20 NGO-led funds2 have emerged, many led by Sudanese actors, and they are expected to channel more than $40 million to local responders in 2026. Together they mark a new and potentially powerful chapter in localization. The SHF brings scale, while these funds can move faster, reach further, and provide assistance beyond an emergency. The SHF, donors, and NGO-led funds should launch a structured dialogue on how they can best fit together.

This report seeks to provide accurate, up-to-date information on the trajectory of the Sudan Humanitarian Fund (SHF), and practical recommendations for accelerating further progress on localization. The SHF has a real opening. The true measure of progress will be whether a much wider group of Sudanese responders receives direct funding, holds real authority over funding decisions, and becomes durable humanitarian actors.

This report was co-authored by the Conflict Sensitivity Facility (CSF), Refugees International3, and an independent consultant, Yousra Semmache. It builds on Refugees International’s September 2025 report, Accelerating Localization: A Roadmap for the Sudan Humanitarian Fund, as well as the SHF “deep dive” report undertaken by national NGOs already onboarded with the Fund in November 2025. Additional desk research reviewed documentation and findings from workshops and surveys held throughout 2025 and 2026, which gauged the views of dozens of Sudanese NGOs and international stakeholders on SHF access, governance, partnership practices, and localization performance.

Between May and July 2026, Refugees International and the CSF interviewed 15 people with direct knowledge of the Fund, including recently retired OCHA personnel and representatives of eight Sudanese NGOs that had either recently completed onboarding or are longstanding SHF partners. The analysis also draws on publicly available data and operational information concerning the Fund’s 2026 allocations, partner assessments, and evolving localization policies. A draft of this report was circulated for comment to participants invited to a July 30 roundtable of Sudanese stakeholders brought together to discuss the legacy of Sudan’s failed 2024 localization reform effort and the current direction of system reform. A draft was also circulated for comment to the SHF. The Fund chose not to provide comments during the review period.

While the SHF made some important strides on localization over the past several years, a key barrier has been the narrow pipeline of eligible Sudanese partners. In 2024, the SHF invited 62 national NGOs into its capacity-assessment and onboarding process, a necessary step to receive direct funding and also advantageous for joining a consortium as an implementing partner. By the end of 2024, just two were accepted as SHF partners. UN staff interviewed in 2025 named the main barrier to approving more Sudanese NGOs: many lacked double-entry bookkeeping systems, a technical gap that is relatively easy to fix. By the end of 2025, the Fund had 25 Sudanese NGO partners, only one more than in 2024, and only six local and national humanitarian actors (L/NAs) received direct grants, according to a March 2026 analysis by ODI Global. Both the overall national partner base and the number of directly funded partners remained well below those of peer funds.

Two prevailing assumptions within the SHF have contributed to the limited number of directly funded Sudanese partners. The first is that many L/NAs do not necessarily want direct funding, whether because of security concerns, fiduciary risk, or capacity constraints. Yet evidence from a 2025 INGO-led workshop dedicated to better understanding how L/NAs view barriers at the SHF complicates that view: among 21 senior representatives from 16 national NGOs, 57 percent had received SHF funding indirectly through international organizations, none had received a direct grant, and all expressed interest in doing so.

A second assumption has been that institutional capacity investment is not a core function of a country-based pooled fund and should instead be left primarily to bilateral donors. In practice, this position has limited the ability of Sudanese NGOs to strengthen the systems and capacities needed to progress from implementing roles into direct, prime recipients of SHF funding. OCHA’s Global Guidance for CBPFs, however, gives pooled funds two mutually reinforcing purposes: financing life-saving humanitarian action and contributing to system change and localization. In this guidance, investments in local and national actors’ capacity and infrastructure are seen to improve lifesaving itself.

CBPFs also routinely finance the considerably more expensive institutional structures of UN agencies and INGOs, including their staffing, compliance, security, and overhead costs. Refusing to invest the same way in L/NAs does not save money for lifesaving aid. Instead, it can lock in costlier delivery models over time and leave less money for affected communities.

The Ukraine Humanitarian Fund (UHF) offers an important counterexample. At the outset of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, relatively few Ukrainian NGOs had significant humanitarian experience, and only a limited number were eligible UHF partners. By investing substantial resources in their institutional capacity and operational systems, however, the Fund helped build a broad and credible pool of national organizations able to manage larger grants directly. This earlier investment enabled the UHF to channel an exceptional share of the recent U.S. allocation to Ukrainian actors. According to a joint analysis by Share Trust and Refugees International of UHF cost structures in 2024, the ability of the UHF to expand reliance on L/NAs meant that tens of millions of dollars in cost savings were available for more lifesaving programming.

title: Sudan: At least 18 children killed in wave of airborne attacks
text:
KHARTOUM, 21 October 2026 – At least 18 children are among hundreds of people reportedly killed in a wave of drone attacks and airstrikes across Sudan in the past week, said Save the Children.

According to the UN, at least 10 children were reportedly killed in drone attacks over the weekend, with a further three children reportedly killed on Monday in the capital Khartoum. On Thursday, five children from the same family were reportedly killed in North Kordofan in an airstrike, with their mother surviving with injuries.

Claire Henery, Save the Children’s Country Director in Sudan, said:

“The recent wave of drone attacks across Sudan is deeply worrying for children and families already living through one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises.

"Beyond the tragic loss of life, these attacks risk further disrupting hospitals, schools and other critical services, endangering children and families already struggling to survive the consequences of war.

“Drones are changing the reality of this conflict for children. With drone and aerial attacks increasingly reaching communities far from active front lines and striking with little warning, children and families can no longer feel safe even in areas previously considered less exposed to conflict. As children return to school, this growing threat adds to their fear and insecurity. Every child should be able to go to school and return home safely.”

Children should never have to live in fear of attack, whether at home, on their way to school, or while accessing healthcare, said Save the Children. The international community cannot look away as civilians continue to bear the brunt of this violence. All parties to the conflict must uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law, protect civilians, and end attacks that put children's lives and futures at risk. Sudan's children have already endured far too much loss, fear and disruption.

The ongoing conflict has caused the world’s largest displacement crisis, forcing about 11 million people from their homes, reducing access to farmland, damaging infrastructure and irrigation systems and causing shortages of seeds, fertilizers and equipment. Last week, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) warned that conflict, displacement and severe El Niño-induced drought are increasing the risk of famine in parts of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan.

Save the Children has worked in Sudan since 1983 and provides programming for children and families affected by conflict, displacement, extreme poverty and hunger.

Minahil* fled her home in Darfur with four of her children as the conflict engulfed the city travelling across the country before finding safety 1000km away in River Nile province where she is being supported by Save the Children. Simon Edmunds / Save the Children

The new arrivals are now part of more than 605,000 people living in El Obeid town and Sheikan locality, who have come seeking safety but are facing new challenges in accessing health, water, education and protection services within the city.

A displacement camp in River Nile province where families who have fled conflict in Sudan are being supported by Save the Children Simon Edmunds / Save the Children

More than 5,500 children are among the 11,000 people newly displaced in the wake of escalating violence in and around the city of El Obeid in North Kordofan, Sudan, with thousands more at risk.

Children should be protected before recruitment begins.Across conflict-affected communities, children face risks that can fundamentally change the course of their lives. Poverty, insecurity, displacement, disrupted education, family separation and limited opportunities can leave children increasingly vulnerable to recruitment and use by armed forces and armed groups.A new research publication, Preventing the Recruitment and Use of Children: An Analysis of the Barriers to Implementing Select Vancouver Principles in South Sudan and Somalia, examines these challenges and asks an important question: What will it take to prevent children from being recruited in the first place?The study looks at the implementation of selected Vancouver Principles in South Sudan and Somalia, two countries where children continue to experience the devastating consequences of armed conflict.

title: WFP Sudan Market Monitor - October 2026
text:
In September 2026, prices of all monitored food commodities in Sudan increased at an unprecedented rate, exceeding levels observed even during the years of widespread conflict. Prices of some food items rose by more than 50 percent compared to August 2026. On a year-on-year basis, staple food prices were between 81 and 176 percent higher than in September 2025. As a result, the national average cost of the WFP Local Food Basket (LFB) reached SDG 4,758, marking a 24 percent increase from August 2026 and a 127 percent increase compared to the same period last year.

The Sudanese Pound continued to depreciate against the US dollar due to persistent conflict-related economic disruptions, the ongoing Middle East crisis, strong demand for foreign currency, and increases in customs exchange rates. In September, the exchange rate averaged SDG 7,500 per USD in the parallel market and SDG 6,500 per USD through commercial banks, reflecting month-on-month depreciations of 22 percent and 18 percent, respectively.

While staple food commodities remained available in most monitored markets, supply levels were generally below normal. This was mainly driven by below-average production during the previous agricultural season, continued disruptions to domestic trade and supply chains, and challenges affecting global supply chains. These factors, combined with the rapid depreciation of the local currency, continued to exert significant upward pressure on food prices across the country.

title: Sudan humanitarian crisis continues amid widespread violence
text:
The EUAA has published two new Country of Origin Information (COI) reports on Sudan, examining political, judicial and human rights developments in the country as well as the socio-economic situation in Khartoum on the one hand (Country Focus report, August 2026) and the security situation on the other (Security Situation report, October 2026).

As violence continues to shape Sudan’s conflict, civilians face large-scale violence, human rights violations and mounting humanitarian needs. The newly published Security Situation report on Sudan examines the country’s security trends and the key actors involved in the conflict at national and regional level. It builds on the EUAA COI Country Focus report on Sudan published in August, which addresses the political, human rights and socio-economic context as well as the treatment of certain profiles and groups of the population in the country.

More than three years into the conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), authority remains increasingly fragmented in the country. International mediation efforts involving the African Union, IGAD, the United States of America, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and Switzerland failed to achieve a lasting ceasefire. Disagreements between external actors, the SAF’s refusal to negotiate with the RSF on equal footing and conflicting political interests, have hindered progress.

Against this backdrop, civilians continue to be significantly impacted by the conflict as widespread human rights violations are reported, including extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances, torture and sexual violence. The number of people at risk of sexual and gender-based violence rose by 350% between 2023 and mid-2025.

The impact of the conflict has been particularly severe in areas subjected to prolonged sieges and intense fighting. El Fasher, the last SAF stronghold in Darfur, fell to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in October 2025 after an 18-months siege. By late September, a 68-kilometres-long earth berm encircled the city, restricting access to food and medicines, trapping civilians and leaving people to starve. The RSF takeover was marked by widespread and systematic violence. In North Kordofan, El Obeid faced siege-like conditions for months, amid increasing use of drones by both parties. Reporting on events around the capture of El Fasher, the UN independent international fact-finding mission (FFM) for the Sudan concluded that the RSF committed crimes against humanity, war crimes and acted with genocidal intent, particularly targeting non-Arab communities, including the Zaghawa.

The humanitarian situation is equally dire. In 2025-2026, approximately 19.5 million people faced acute food insecurity and several areas in the country were affected by famine or the risk of it. Around 17 million people lacked access to safe drinking water, increasing the risk of disease outbreaks and malnutrition. At the same time, the conflict damaged agricultural infrastructure and disrupted supply chains, while rising food prices worsened hunger. Humanitarian assistance was severely restricted by armed attacks, bureaucratic barriers, blocked roads, and insufficient funding. By April 2026, an estimated 70% of Sudan's population was living in poverty, while, as of February 2026, around 29 million people required humanitarian food assistance.

EU Asylum situation for Sudan nationals

Between March 2025 and August 2026, Sudanese nationals lodged around 31,000 asylum applications in the EU+. Over three quarters of them were received by Greece (13,000) and France (11,000). Sudanese applications began to climb at the start of the conflict in April 2023 and rose sharply during 2025, reaching a record high in October. In the first eight months of 2026, the upward trend continued with 15,000 applications lodged in total, an increase of almost two thirds compared to the same period in 2025. This has made Sudan the top fifth nationality applying for asylum in the EU+ so far this year. During the reporting period, EU+ countries issued around 20,000 first instance decisions to Sudanese nationals, with an overall recognition rate of 66%. Greece (8,000) and France (7,900) issued the most decisions. At the start of August 2026, over 11,000 cases were pending a decision at first instance, around half of them in Greece (5,400).

The EUAA regularly updates its Country-of-Origin Information reports, which aim to provide accurate and reliable up-to-date information on third countries to support EU+ asylum and migration authorities in reaching accurate and fair decisions in asylum procedures, as well as to support national policymaking.

title: At least 12 children reportedly killed in separate incidents in West Kordofan and Khartoum, Sudan [EN/AR]
text:
KHARTOUM, 20 October 2026 – At least 12 children, some as young as two, were reportedly killed in two separate incidents in Sudan's West Kordofan and Khartoum states in recent days.

On Saturday, 17 October, at least nine children – five boys and four girls, aged between five and ten – were killed in an attack on a camp for displaced families east of Sanakit, in West Kordofan State.

Two days later, on Monday, 19 October, an armed drone struck a residential area in Khartoum, reportedly killing three children – two girls and one boy aged between two and six – along with their father.

"In West Kordofan, children were killed in a camp their families had fled to for safety. In Khartoum, three young children were reportedly killed with their father in their own neighbourhood, in a city where many families have returned to rebuild their lives," said Angela Kearney, UNICEF Acting Representative in Sudan. "Families in Sudan are doing everything they can to keep their children safe, whether by fleeing or by going home. Neither is protecting them. Every party to this conflict must protect children, wherever they are."

Across Sudan, children continue to face deadly violence after more than three years of conflict. For families who have already endured displacement and immense hardship, even places of shelter offer no guarantee of safety.

UNICEF calls on all parties to the conflict to comply with their obligations under international humanitarian law and protect civilians and civilian infrastructure. Children must be protected wherever they are, at all times.

title: War and El Niño-driven drought deplete food stocks, pushing Sudan further towards famine, new data finds
text:
The latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) alert shows nearly three years of war and a severe El Niño drought are depleting food stocks in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, where over 300,000 people have been displaced since October

Food is running out and acute malnutrition is rising, with the risk of famine growing in parts of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan.

Donors must scale up funding for food, health and nutrition, and parties to the conflict must end attacks on civilians and allow safe access.

Khartoum, Sudan, October 13, 2026 — El Niño-induced drought is compounding conflict and driving a growing risk of famine as conditions rapidly deteriorate in parts of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, Sudan, warns the latest IPC alert. Child acute malnutrition is already above the famine threshold in two camps in South Darfur, with child mortality rates in the surveyed camps reaching emergency levels. The International Rescue Committee (IRC) is calling on donors to scale up funding for food, health and nutrition, and on parties to the conflict to allow safe, unimpeded humanitarian access. Across Sudan, harvests are expected to be near record-poor and food stocks are being depleted as prices climb. Acute food insecurity remains severe in North Darfur, where delayed rains devastated crop cultivation and forced many displaced farmers to buy food. Ongoing conflict and shifting frontlines add to the danger: even where crops have been planted, the coming season carries serious risks. With drought growing in nearby areas, Tawila, which already hosts more than 650,000 internally displaced people, could see a surge in arrivals as people seek food, water and other basic services.

“In Sudan, years of conflict mean El Niño brings hunger immediately,” said Richard Data, IRC’s country director in Sudan. “This famine warning should be a wake-up call for donors to immediately scale up humanitarian funding for emergency food, health and nutrition assistance.”

The IRC and other humanitarian agencies are racing against time as needs in Sudan outpace response capacity. More than 5 million people already face emergency levels of hunger, and an estimated 825,000 children under five are expected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition. These new devastating developments reflect the cumulative impact of more than three years of relentless conflict, economic collapse and shrinking humanitarian access that have pushed millions of families in Sudan to the brink, and have led Sudan to top IRC’s Emergency Watchlist for three consecutive years.

Emergency aid alone is not enough. The IRC is calling on all parties to the conflict to allow safe, unimpeded humanitarian access to people in areas of active fighting and to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure. International donors must also restore predictable funding and scale up humanitarian action. Without an urgent response, even more lives will be lost, and more communities pushed into famine.

The IRC scaled up our response in Sudan in 2023 when the conflict began. We now work in Blue Nile, Gedaref, Khartoum, River Nile, White Nile, South Kordofan, North Darfur, Central Darfur and West Darfur providing healthcare, nutrition treatment for children and pregnant and lactating women, access to water and sanitation, protection services for women and children, and cash assistance.

title: Sudan: Drought and war push Darfur and Kordofan towards famine
text:
The risk of famine is growing in parts of Sudan already torn apart by war, as a severe El Niño drought makes life even harder in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, the UN-backed global hunger monitor warned on Monday.

In a new alert, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said fresh evidence shows malnutrition getting worse in several hotspots. Aid is not keeping up, held back by a severe lack of funding, insecurity and restricted access.

The IPC food insecurity alert index is a global partnership that includes the UN emergency food agency WFP and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).

In Eastern Jebel Marra, South Darfur, a survey of two camps for displaced people found acute malnutrition among children at 38 and 30.8 per cent – above the threshold for famine. Hunger was severe and death rates were high.

Across Greater Darfur, 13 of the 17 nutrition surveys carried out since January found critical levels of acute malnutrition.

In Nyala, the share of children seeking nutrition help who needed treatment for severe acute malnutrition more than doubled between January and August, from five to 11 per cent.

Drought now covers more than half of Sudan, wiping out crops in some areas and leaving families without food or income.

In North Darfur, 64 per cent of cropland is showing poor plant growth.

Rains arrived in late September, too late to save most cereal crops, the alert said, and cereal prices are very likely to keep rising.

Greater Kordofan, described in the alert as the epicentre of Sudan’s conflict, has seen more than 300,000 people forced from their homes since October 2025. Markets have been hit by more than 170 airstrikes, looting incidents or armed clashes this year.

Aid workers face extreme danger. Two trucks contracted by WFP came under fire on 2 and 3 October, killing at least one person.

Children are going without treatment. As of August, only 26 per cent of those expected to need care for severe acute malnutrition with medical complications had received it. Without treatment, as many as two thirds of them could die.

As of 8 October, less than half of the humanitarian appeal for Sudan had been funded.

The IPC’s Famine Review Committee said there is not enough survey data for a full analysis, but the evidence points to a rapidly worsening situation.

“Famine is the collapse of systems,” the committee said. “We are witnessing a humanitarian catastrophe, already of historic proportions.”

The alert called for an end to the fighting, safe and sustained access for aid agencies – especially in North and West Kordofan – and flexible funding on a large scale. Without a major increase in help, it warned, more lives will be at risk.

title: IPC Sudan Food Insecurity and Malnutrition Alert
text:
The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), of which WHO is a member, today issued a Food Insecurity and Malnutrition Alert for Sudan.

The IPC is warning of a growing risk of famine across parts of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, where conflict, mass displacement, severe drought and inadequate humanitarian funding are driving a rapidly deteriorating situation.

An El Niño-induced drought, affecting roughly half of the country, is compounding the impacts of conflict and displacement, reducing food availability, driving up prices and affecting livelihoods. The IPC Alert highlights alarming levels of acute food insecurity and malnutrition in several localities, including new areas of concern.

Health care is extremely limited, often entirely inaccessible, while clean water is becoming increasingly scarce, leaving a poorly nourished population highly vulnerable to disease and death.

End hostilities, safeguard civilians, and protect food, water and health systems;

secure safe and sustained humanitarian access in frontline areas, especially in North and West Kordofan;

WHO is supporting the health and nutrition response across Sudan, including treating medical complications in children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and responding to disease outbreaks. Hunger and malnutrition compound the effects of diseases on affected communities as malnourished people are more susceptible to developing severe forms of diseases such as cholera and measles.

In 2026, WHO has provided training, supplies and other support to all 161 operational nutrition stabilization centres across the country, helping treat over 26 000 children with SAM and medical complications between January and August.

The health system remains severely weakened by conflict, displacement, attacks on health care and chronic funding shortages. Since 15 April 2023, WHO has verified 228 attacks on health care that have led to 2055 deaths and 817 injuries. By 2026, 37% of the country’s health facilities had stopped functioning.

With only 23% of its US$ 97.7 million humanitarian appeal funded, WHO is calling for increased funding and sustained humanitarian access to expand essential health, nutrition and hygiene services to prevent further deterioration.

The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) is an innovative multi-stakeholder global initiative aimed at enhancing food security and nutrition analysis to inform decisions. Learn more.

title: UN agencies warn humanitarian system in Sudan ‘could collapse’
text:
UN aid agencies on Monday said they may be forced to scale back humanitarian aid in Sudan – home of the world’s worst hunger and displacement crisis – due to funding shortfalls.

“We simply can’t turn our back on the people of Sudan when they need us most,” Director General of the UN migration agency (IOM) Amy Pope said on Monday. The entire humanitarian system could collapse within weeks if we don't act now."

Sudan has been embroiled in a brutal civil conflict since 2023 between rival militaries and their backers. Some 8.6 million people remain internally displaced and 19.5 million people currently face crisis levels of food insecurity, which has been compounded by maritime disruptions and drought caused by the El Niño weather pattern.

Speaking to reporters on Monday following an eight-day trip to Sudan, WFP Acting Director Carl Skau said the crisis in Sudan “by far does not get the attention it deserves.”

He added that WFP has the presence and capacity to deliver an effective humanitarian response but is mostly constrained by funding.

“It is possible to make a difference,” he said. “Our main problem is funding. There is a risk we will have to scale back quite significantly in the next few weeks unless more funding is provided.”

The Common Humanitarian Pipeline system – managed by IOM and allowing more than 100 partners to provide aid – has reached 2.84 million people since July 2023. But its reach has shrunk each year due to falling donations as other crises dominate global attention.

IOM warned that current shelter, sanitation and emergency household relief items will run out by the end of September, while warehouses will close without additional funding by December.

Meanwhile, WFP reaches 4 to 5 million people in Sudan each month with humanitarian aid, including agricultural support and cash and food assistance.

Amid access challenges by road, Mr. Skau said WFP recently expanded its humanitarian aid service in Sudan. With additional humanitarian funding, the UN and its partners could expand the air service and reach more civilians in need.

“We need to step up,” Mr. Skau said. “We cannot continue to fail these people.”

Well into its fourth year, the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) continues to endanger civilians and drive people from their homes, according to the UN’s aid office (OCHA).

Over the weekend, drone strikes displaced thousands across the states of Blue Nile, North Darfur and West Darfur. Local sources reported civilian casualties.

In North Kordofan, El Obeid has acted as a haven for people fleeing violence elsewhere in the country. But the RSF has surrounded the city, and camps for internally displaced people (IDPs) are stretched beyond their capacities, putting increasing pressure on essential services.

“We once again call on all parties to the conflict to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and to allow rapid, safe, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access to all those in need across Sudan,” OCHA said.

On a recent eight-day trip to Sudan, Mr. Skau visited communities and local displacement camps in El Obeid, El Fasher, Khartoum and other areas.

He told reporters that he spoke with women who had to return home without water after a tank ran out and people who walked up to five days to reach IDP camps after their villages were destroyed.

In the North Darfur town of Tawila, Mr. Skau said he saw hundreds of thousands who had fled violence in El Fasher living in “an endless ocean of grass huts.” WFP has reached nearly the entire population with assistance but is only able to provide half rations.

It took Mr. Skau three days to travel by car from El Obeid to El Fasher – a journey which he said used to take six hours.

Upon his arrival in El Fasher, Mr. Skau found a “daunting city” hollowed out by the RSF’s brutal 18-month siege on the city, which ended in late October.

“I have seen a lot in this job and beyond. El Fasher was quite special,” Mr. Skau said. “It illustrates what conflict leaves behind, and it underlines the urgency of bringing an end to the conflict.”

When displaced families do not receive adequate shelter, they face increased risk of gender-based violence, family separation and eviction from overcrowded IDP camps.

IOM requires $15 million to maintain its humanitarian pipeline at minimum capacity for 12 months, though additional funding would allow it to reach more people.

WFP is only about one-third funded in Sudan, according to Mr. Skau. More donations would allow the agency to more effectively provide for locals’ needs and adequately protect civilians.

“People deserve to be supported with basic humanitarian assistance,” Mr. Skau said.

title: Human rights chief Türk renews call for end to spiralling Sudan war
text:
The ongoing war in Sudan took centre stage at the UN Human Rights Council on Monday where the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, led calls for an end to attacks on civilians in “markets, hospitals [and] fuel stations”.

Türk calls for an immediate ceasefire and end to foreign involvement

Civilians face growing attacks, including from long-range drones

Now well into its fourth year, the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created a massive humanitarian emergency, with more than six million people displaced internally and another 4.5 million forced to seek shelter across Sudan’s borders.

In his appeal for an end to the violence, UN rights chief Mr. Türk warned about the deteriorating situation in Kordofan, Blue Nile, and North and West Darfur, stressing that civilians remain at “imminent” risk.

“There needs to be an immediate ceasefire, an end to foreign involvement, and a return to inclusive civilian rule,” he insisted.

The High Commissioner’s appeal follows the publication of a new report into the conflict by senior independent investigators appointed by the Human Rights Council. The investigators are not UN staff and they are not paid for their work.

Their key findings include the increasing use of long-range drones against civilians and the significant support allegedly provided to paramilitary rebel fighters by “individuals and entities” in the United Arab Emirates, Chad, southeastern Libya and Puntland in Somalia.

“Both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are increasingly using long-range drones, resulting in attacks now reaching far beyond traditional front lines,” said Mohamed Othman, chair of the Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan, which was created by the Council in Geneva in October 2023.

Mr. Othman also stressed that drone strikes had injured and killed civilians “in their homes, schools, hospitals, markets, displacement sites and places of refuge and while attending weddings, funerals and other community gatherings”.

Turning to El Obeid city in North Kordofan, where access is heavily contested, the human rights investigator warned that “repeated RSF drone attacks” had impacted water, energy and other vital civilian infrastructure.

“These attacks underscore that these risks remain acute, as civilians continue to face repeated aerial threats, displacement and pressure on already strained essential services”, he said, in a city under partial siege by the RSF.

The fact-finding mission’s report highlights how both parties to the conflict have carried out attacks on civilians.

These included “successive” RSF drone strikes on a kindergarten and a hospital in Kalogie, South Kordofan, that left 114 dead including 60 children, along with SAF attacks on Ad-Da'ein Teaching Hospital that killed at least 70 people.

“Based on the evidence gathered, we found reasonable grounds to believe that both the SAF and the RSF committed serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law which may amount to war crimes,” Mr. Othman told the Council.

In a separate update from Khartoum, the UN World Health Organization (WHO) reported on Monday that the devastation of three key hospitals in the capital has been repeated across the country.

Before the conflict, Khartoum Teaching Hospital, the Ophthalmology Hospital and the Dental Hospital were major referral and teaching hospitals. Today, their buildings and medical equipment have sustained extensive damage.

“Operating theatres have been destroyed, imaging equipment lost and several wards have collapsed,” said WHO Representative in Sudan, Dr Abdinasir Abubakar. “Entire blocks and departments are out of service. The buildings need urgent structural repair before patients can be admitted safely.”

Despite the difficult working conditions, hospital staff remain present to treat patients “in the parts of the buildings that remain usable”, Dr Abubakar continued, in an appeal for assistance to repair the “immense” damage.

title: Fighting deepens needs and fuels further displacement in Sudan
text:
Ongoing conflict, displacement and funding shortages continue to deepen needs in Sudan, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned on Monday, underscoring the need for greater civilian protection.

RSF drone attacks continue on El Obeid, capital of North Kordofan, where humanitarians continue to scale up support despite serious security challenges

Fighting in West Darfur has displaced some 18,000 people from more than 20 villages in the past week alone, most fleeing across the border into Chad

Funding shortfalls have forced the closure of three health facilities in Central Darfur, cutting off some 75,000 displaced people from essential care

Sudan's $3 billion humanitarian appeal is only 40 per cent funded, with $1.2 billion received so far this year

OCHA drew particular attention to the situation around El Obeid, capital of North Kordofan state, where insecurity continues to endanger civilians and drive displacement.

People are flocking to the city and surrounding areas in search of safety and assistance.

Despite the challenging environment, the UN and partners are reaching people in El Obeid.

They have provided two million litres of drinking water to about 133,000 people amid severe water shortages.

Meanwhile, UN migration agency IOM reported that fighting in Sirba locality, West Darfur state, has displaced roughly 18,000 people from more than 20 villages since last week. Most have reportedly fled across the border into Chad.

The war in Sudan shows no signs of stopping as the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and former allies the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) remain locked in a brutal battle for power.

The war erupted in April 2023, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. More than 30 million people need humanitarian assistance and more than nine million people are displaced within the country.

OCHA once again called on all parties to protect civilians and to facilitate rapid, safe, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access.

At the same time, funding gaps are limiting the assistance available to people in need, the agency added.

Funding shortfalls forced the recent closure of three health facilities in Central Darfur state, leaving some 75,000 displaced people without adequate access to essential health services.

OCHA continues to urge donors to provide additional support for the humanitarian response in Sudan.

A nearly $3 billion appeal to meet needs this year is just over 40 per cent funded, with $1.2 billion received to date.

As the war grinds on, the UN remains committed to achieving de-escalation.

The Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy for Sudan, Pekka Haavisto, continues to engage the parties.

He “has been able to have meetings with both of the sides, and is trying to work with them,” UN Deputy Spokesperson Farhan Haq told journalists in New York.

The Envoy also continues to work with UN partners, including the African Union, the League of Arab States, and the East African bloc IGAD “to actually get a full cessation of hostilities and progress in negotiations between the parties.”

title: WFP warns El Obeid is becoming the new epicentre of Sudan's displacement and hunger crisis
text:
The city of El Obeid is hosting hundreds of thousands of internally displaced people, possibly doubling the size of the city, and placing additional pressures on already overstretched resources and services. Food, fuel, and water supplies are scarce.

Camps for displaced families in the city are beyond capacity and new families are arriving daily, coming from the Kordofan’s and even as far as Darfur.

Further displacement and destruction of livelihoods will significantly worsen food security in the whole region and increase the risk of malnutrition among young children and pregnant and breastfeeding mothers and girls.

Regular power outages are disrupting water supplies in El Obeid, contributing to shortages of safe drinking water. More than 30 new cholera cases have been recorded.

Nearly 400,000 people across Sheikan district, which includes El Obeid, as well as neighbouring Bara and Gharb Bara districts, are already experiencing emergency levels of acute food insecurity (IPC 4). This means they need immediate food assistance to prevent hunger-related deaths.

WFP is assisting just over 100,000 people in El Obeid, primarily with food but also some cash assistance. Severe funding shortfalls mean people only receive 50 percent rations.

In some cases, people are sharing their limited food rations with other families in need, further reducing overall food support they receive.

Commercial transport within El Obeid has become a challenge due to a lack of fuel.

WFP trucks are helping to move 200 metric tons of food each day from NGO partner warehouses to food distribution points.

In May, the WFP-led Logistics Cluster launched common storage services in El Obeid, providing partners with 500 square metres of storage space for lifesaving relief supplies used by humanitarian partners.

Food stocks are being positioned to scale-up the provision of hot meals and in-kind food assistance to more than 250,000 people in or around El Obeid, if conditions allow.

Supplies for a potential El Obeid response have been redirected from stocks originally intended for rainy season prepositioning. This means WFP will not be able to support communities as planned during the rainy season, which has already begun in parts of the country.

WFP’s Sudan operation is under severe strain. More than 19.5 million people are acutely food insecure - including an estimated 770,000 in 14 locations at risk of famine - but WFP has only been able to reach an average of 3 million people each month due to access and funding constraints.

Armed clashes, drone strikes, and insecurity continue to restrict humanitarian movements and limit WFP’s ability to reach priority populations. In June alone, active conflict prevented WFP from delivering lifesaving assistance to an estimated 200,000 people.

Critical funding shortfalls are putting continued food assistance at risk. Based on current planning for lifesaving operations, WFP’s food stocks will be severely depleted by September and fully exhausted in October. Specialized food to prevent and treat malnutrition will start running out in August.

WFP requires USD 646 million from June to November 2026 to reach a planned 8.5 million people with lifesaving assistance and support to rebuild food production.

Without sustained funding and safe access, hard-won gains in the fight against hunger risk being reversed, including in areas where regular WFP assistance has helped reduce the risk of famine.
